articles.title_orig: BIO pitches US plan to beat China in biotech ‘space race’
articles.title_zh: BIO pitches US plan to beat China in biotech ‘space race’
articles.content_orig:
iStock, CHOMCHILAI PHONHARN
Leaders of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization are calling on the Trump administration to establish a new White House Office of Biotechnology and ease clinical trial requirements in an effort to stem the flow of Chinese innovation that puts American companies at risk.
The industry group rolled out the detailed plan to Tuesday fight back in “our generation’s Space Race,” according to the release.
“If China becomes the world’s biotech leader, it could threaten our national security, cost countless jobs, and leave us dependent on an adversary for life-saving medicines,” BIO CEO John Crowley said in a statement. “Washington policymakers need to act.”
Annalee Armstrong, BioSpace
The plan includes seven pillars meant to coordinate a national strategy to boost the American biotech ecosystem, accelerate medical breakthroughs and support future research, manufacturing and intellectual property protections.
A new White House Office of Biotechnology would replicate similar offices for other key industry sectors like the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office to coordinate policy across the federal government, the plan suggests. This office would be responsible for developing a national biotech strategy and providing reports on the state of the industry.
BIO also wants to boost clinical trial abilities by accelerating first-in-human research, advancing alternatives to animal testing and removing regulatory barriers to testing. The plan also recommends streamlining institutional review boards and cutting delays in contracting and site activation. These same policies were suggested by leaders on a webinar hosted by BioSpace in October and to some degree are supported by recent FDA initiatives .
The plan also recommends building out a resilient network of U.S. manufacturing, providing an alternative to Chinese contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs) that have become the target of U.S. restrictions.
Assets from China comprise 56% of the total licensing deal value so far this year, according to a recent report by Truist Securities, up from 10% in 2021. Chinese companies have snagged $59 billion in deal value in 2026, while U.S. companies have collected just $35 billion. Much of the deal values for the Chinese firms is made up of long-term milestones, Truist said. About $21 billion has been paid out in upfront payments, with a total of $239 billion that could flow into China in the coming years.
In an effort to stem the tide, the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out a proposal to restrict outbound biotechnology investments in October. The proposal comes from the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act, which was passed by Congress in the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. Trump signed the COINS Act into law in December 2025.
Deals with Chinese biotechs are likely to slow down at least temporarily while the industry digests the impacts of the COINS Act, Truist said, though the restrictions specifically exempt licensing transactions.
Industry leaders like Crowley have been calling for a coordinated response to boost American biotech, just as China has done .
“The biotechnology race is this generation’s space race,” the plan states. “The country that wins will not only shape the future of medicine. It will gain an enduring economic and national security advantage. Success will take an all-of-government effort that unites policymakers, industry, and the research community.”

articles.title_orig: U.S., Russia and Ukraine begin talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: U.S., Russia and Ukraine begin talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions and other restrictions were working so effectively.
"The economic campaign [against Iran] is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations," Rubio said after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris. "That's what I told our allies here today."
President Trump "has concluded that for the time being there is no need for major combat operations because we are achieving the same objective by economic means," Rubio said.
But if Iran crosses "red lines," the "U.S. military stands ready," Rubio added, warning of a "terrible price" for Tehran.
European members of the G7 had pressed Rubio at the meeting in Paris to avoid any new escalation against Iran.
Mr. Trump said Monday the U.S. was keeping the Iran war at "status quo," but warned that American forces were "locked and loaded."
Iran's Houthi allies have denied targeting Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline in the Medina region, saying they instead targeted the vital piece of infrastructure near the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The Saudi energy ministry said Monday that a " limited fire " had broken out on a section of the pipeline after it was targeted, saying there were no deaths or injuries.
In a post on X Tuesday, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group had struck "several pumping stations" along the pipeline in the Riyadh area, but added: "The Saudi enemy's latest false accusation – that we targeted the East-West pipeline in Medina – is a blatant and enormous lie."
The Saudis have accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, multiple times since the fighting between the two sides reignited in summer, which the Houthis have stringently denied.
An attack on the pipeline in September , which Saudi Arabia blamed on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, put the pipeline out of action for several weeks.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, facing an impeachment effort by the soon to be-Democratically controlled U.S. Congress, repeated his frequent claim on Tuesday that the U.S. had won the war with Iran. Even as Tehran claimed four more ships were stopped by attacks, Hegseth declared the Strait of Hormuz under U.S. control.
"In Operation Epic Fury, by every measure, we achieved a historic MILITARY VICTORY," Hegseth said in remarks during a briefing that the Pentagon shared on social media .
"Their navy sunk. Their air force grounded. Their defense industrial base — gone. More than 80 percent of their nuclear industrial base — gone. Their military in ruin. The ironclad blockade, UNBROKEN," declared Hegseth, adding: "We control the Strait of Hormuz."
All of the embattled defense chief's assertions have been disputed by Iran, where officials claimed only a month ago that the Islamic Republic's weapons production capacity had increased by 250% since the war began, with help from Russia and China.
The commander of the U.S. military's Central Command said he had flown over the Strait of Hormuz in October and seen no Iranian Revolutionary Guard vessels, and he declared U.S.-protected shipping lanes through the vital waterway "free and clear." But Iran has continued to claim daily attacks on commercial vessels that use those shipping lanes, both with missiles and sea mines.
On Iran's nuclear program, much of it was seriously damaged a year before the U.S. and Israel launched the current war, when they carried out a series of previous strikes in June 2025. U.N. experts believe Iran still has about 972 pounds of 60% enriched uranium, a short step away from the 90% enrichment levels needed for high-yield military warheads, but that it is likely buried under one of the facilities damaged in 2025.
Iran has not, after more than eight months of war, agreed to any renewed monitoring of its nuclear program, or to the removal of its highly-enriched uranium , as part of any potential peace deal.
A top Iranian security official claimed late Monday that the U.S. has been "wrecked" by its war against Iran and declared it time for the Trump administration to "surrender" and accept Tehran's terms to end the conflict.
Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, said on X that the U.S. must accept the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly laid out as its core terms for any peace deal.
"The war on Iran has already wrecked the U.S. government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler. FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks. Stop denying the West Asian NEW ORDER," he wrote. "Time to SURRENDER to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out."
President Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday that he believed the war with Iran "militarily, is effectively over," suggesting that, for now, he is not prepared to resume airstrikes.
Iran's longstanding demands, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed this week as "unacceptable," include an end to the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, an end to fighting on all fronts, including Israel's war with Hezbollah in Lebanon, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and gas sales and release of Iranian state funds held abroad, war reparations and other measures.
The European Union said Tuesday that it was ready to mount a fast and "united response" after France blamed Iran for a cyberattack that targeted hundreds of grocery stores in the country last month.
"We acknowledge that France has attributed this to Iran. Pending discussions with member states, we, as the European Union, stand ready to come with a swift and united response," EU spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.
The Paris prosecutor's office said Monday that French officials believed a cyber unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had carried out the Oct. 11 hacks that caused temperatures in refrigeration units at some 700 grocery stores to surge, wasting tons of food and causing about 20 fires.
Multiple explosions were heard over Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh early Tuesday, as the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said it shot down a missile targeting the city, which has suffered weeks of disruptive attacks.
Journalists working for the French news agency AFP heard several blasts as residents received a cell phone alert urging them to shelter from an "aerial threat." The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, has faced near-daily Houthi strikes since early October, including attacks that killed 20 people and closed Riyadh's airport for two weeks.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Tuesday that two more oil tankers attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz were "halted by powerful explosions and left burning."
The IRGC said in a statement that one of the vessels struck a naval mine, while the other was under the protection of U.S. fighter jets when it "suffered an incident and was brought to a halt at its location amid a massive fire."
Both Iran and the U.S. have been attacking ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz for weeks, accusing the vessels of breaching their respective restrictions on access to the waterway.
The IRGC said the tankers affected Tuesday had been traveling through what Tehran considers unauthorized shipping lanes close to Oman's coast in the southern part of the vital waterway, which the U.S. insists are safe and open.
Iran has warned repeatedly that the southern route is "unsafe" and that all vessels working with the U.S. "will meet the same fate."
The price of oil continued its more than week-long downward trend Tuesday, as markets appeared optimistic that a return to a full-scale U.S. war with Iran was not imminent.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic eyes $1.4 trillion IPO valuation in test of Wall Street's AI fervor
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic eyes $1.4 trillion IPO valuation in test of Wall Street's AI fervor
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (Â£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.
It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.
Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.
Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

articles.title_zh: Chinese Israel envoy rejects claims Beijing provides military assistance to Iran
articles.content_orig:
Shelves were left bare by the cyber-attacks
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.content_orig:
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., said on a Tuesday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.
And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.
"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.
"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."
Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday.
The New York Times reported that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia opened an investigation into its CEO on Sunday. The two Huangs are not related.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"
Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.

articles.title_orig: GTA VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming for Xbox One consoles
articles.title_zh: GTA VI will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming for Xbox One consoles
articles.content_orig:
Rockstar Games confirms GTA VI will run at 30fps across all consoles.
Rockstar Games confirms GTA VI will run at 30fps across all consoles.
Rockstar Games is making Grand Theft Auto VI available on Xbox Cloud Gaming when it launches next week. While you’d normally assume that would mean Grand Theft Auto VI would be available to stream on PCs, the web, Xbox consoles, and even TVs, it appears to be restricted to just Xbox Series X / S and Xbox One consoles.
That does mean that anyone with an older Xbox One console can stream Grand Theft Auto VI instead of having to upgrade to a PS5 or Xbox Series S / X console to play. Rockstar notes that Xbox Cloud Gaming will use the Xbox Series S graphics settings to stream to Xbox consoles. It also means that Microsoft effectively has an exclusive on streaming Grand Theft Auto VI from the cloud for launch, albeit only to Xbox consoles.
I originally reported last month that Microsoft had secured exclusive Grand Theft Auto VI cloud streaming rights, but Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft wouldn’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI exclusively. While Microsoft’s contract might not specifically state exclusive, the end result is exclusive cloud gaming on Xbox, for now. Sony may well eventually announce its own cloud streaming plans for the game, but Rockstar Games notes that Grand Theft Auto VI “will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.” That’s not cloud streaming, though.
I also initially reported that Grand Theft Auto VI would be available to stream on PC, simply because the entire point of Xbox Cloud Gaming is to make games available on Xbox consoles, TVs, PCs, and the web. It’s strange to see a rare exception for Grand Theft Auto VI , but not entirely surprising. Perhaps Microsoft will eventually be able to stream the PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI whenever it launches.
Rockstar Games also confirms Grand Theft Auto VI will run at 30fps across PS5, PS5 Pro, Xbox Series S / X consoles. The main advantage of a PS5 Pro is ray-traced shadows and support for PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR).

articles.title_orig: Stocks, Bonds Fall as CPI Data Fuel Fed-Hike Bets: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks, Bonds Fall as CPI Data Fuel Fed-Hike Bets: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks slipped Tuesday as investors digested a hotter-than-expected inflation report that cemented bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) and S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) each fell 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 0.6% after a sharp rally across the market on Monday.
The Consumer Price Index , released on Tuesday morning, showed prices rose 0.4% in October from a month earlier, higher than the 0.3% economists were expecting but cooler than September's 0.6% gain. October's CPI report did not include annual inflation figures because last year's government shutdown limited the data available.
Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Fed to hike interest rates by 25 basis points, with a subset of Fed watchers expecting a 50 basis point jumbo hike. Recent comments by Fed governor Chris Waller reinforced those bets , as he noted he would be open to a larger hike.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) investors continue to reel from the board's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang following reports of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia stock continued to edge lower on Tuesday morning after falling over 4% the day before.
In other tech news, Anthropic began its roadshow and released an updated filing ahead of its highly anticipated IPO . The AI lab is forging ahead with its public debut despite recent tech stock volatility and is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion.
Oil prices are falling, with Brent crude ( BZ=F ), the international benchmark, and WTI crude ( CL=F ), the US benchmark, declining by around 3%.
While most of the third quarter earnings season is in the rearview mirror, Nvidia-backed neocloud CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and quantum computing stocks Quantum ( QBTS ) and Rigetti Computing ( RGTI ) report results after the bell today.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock extended its decline Tuesday, falling more than 3% after dropping 4% in the prior session.
The stock came under pressure amid a broader market sell-off and growing concerns about increased scrutiny of the chipmaker following CEO Jensen Huang's admission to an affair believed to involve a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferré has the latest:
The scrutiny could center on Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Huang previously worked, and on whether she helped divert restricted Nvidia chips to China. The Information reported Tuesday that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia hardware had been shipped to Chinese companies through a network linked to Alice Huang since 2023, citing two people familiar with the matter.
On Monday, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Congress needs more answers about the matter, adding that there are "real ⁠concerns that need to be addressed with respect to the ​Nvidia situation."
US stocks opened lower on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected inflation data strengthened expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.2%, while those on the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 0.8% after stocks rallied on Monday.
Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from the prior month, above economists' expectations for a 0.3% increase. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%, also hotter than forecast.
The report pushed Treasury yields higher, strengthening bets on another Fed rate hike in December. The move comes after stocks saw a sharp stock rally on Monday as oil prices continued to fall.
Shorter-term Treasury yields jumped sharply after the CPI inflation data was released, keeping the pressure on the Fed to raise rates at its next meeting.
The 5-year yield ( ^FVX ) jumped 10 basis points to 4.75%, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.93%. The 30-year yield ( ^TYX ) increased 3 basis points to 5.29%.
Traders now see an 84% chance that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December. Bets that the Fed will hike by 50 basis points jumped from 0% yesterday to 15% today.
The move comes after Fed governor Chris Waller said he would be open to a jumbo 50 basis point rate hike in December if inflation came in hot.
"Inflation is too high … this means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said in a speech in London.
He added that if the October inflation data comes out higher than expected, then stronger action may be needed. "In that case, I believe a 50-basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting," Waller said. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
The latest CPI data is out, and the report showed that inflation came in hotter than expected in October but still cooled from the previous month.
Yahoo Finance's Claire Boston reports:
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October from a month earlier, higher than the 0.3% economists were expecting but below September's 0.6% gain. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, coming in above the 0.2% economists were expecting to match September's levels.
October's report didn't include annual inflation figures because the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to publish full October 2025 data due to the government shutdown last year. But some economists estimate that inflation accelerated slightly on a year-over-year basis.
Rising energy prices weighed heavily on September's report , but October's price increases were less dramatic. Energy costs rose 0.7% last month, down from 5.2% in September.
Housing costs were a major contributor to October's price increases, rising 0.3%, while food costs were up 0.5%.
Anthropic took one step closer to one of the largest initial public offerings in history on Tuesday, unveiling that it plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece.
The Claude chatbot maker could raise as much as $64.4 billion through the offering, valuing the company at more than $1 trillion at the top of the proposed range, according to its updated IPO paperwork
The new terms follow an unusual reversal late Monday, when Anthropic circulated and then retracted earlier IPO details indicating it would sell roughly 867 million shares at $70 to $80 each, according to a Reuters report . The company told bankers those figures were inaccurate.
The offering comes amid growing Wall Street concerns about AI valuations and the enormous spending required to develop the technology.
Separately, Anthropic has secured $26 billion in planned investments from seven technology companies, including Google, Nvidia and Microsoft, through a private placement tied to the IPO.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the public offering.
With 2026 in its final stretch, Wall Street looks poised for another banner pay year.
Bonuses for most finance workers, which will be doled out by early 2027, are projected to rise for a third straight year. That's according to third quarter projections published Tuesday by Johnson Associates, a Wall Street pay consultancy that has for over three decades charted annual compensation for finance workers.
"We were not expecting 2026 to be as good a year for pay as it turned out to be," Alan Johnson, the firm's founder and president, said in an interview. "We're at the top of the mountain," he added.
The odds of a Fed rate hike are creeping upward . A strong jobs report last week cemented the argument further for another raise, Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban reports:
And inflation figures coming later today are expected to confirm that pricing pressures remain stubbornly high.
Together, that's a compelling case — elevated pricing pressures call for a hike, while healthy jobs figures provide cover for tamping down the economy.

articles.title_orig: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.title_zh: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.content_orig:
FILE - In this photo provided by the North Korean government, its leader Kim Jong Un, center, and his daughter, reportedly named Kim Ju Ae, visit a military training base in North Korea, Thursday, March 19, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. 朝鮮通信社/KCNA via KNS via AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.
Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.
"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.
The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.
To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.
Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.
"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.
Tae Yongho, a former minister of North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016, speaks during an interview with The Associated Press in Seoul, South Korea, Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Lee Jin-man/AP hide caption
Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.
Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.
"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.
Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."
Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.
North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.
During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.
The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.
"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.
"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

articles.title_zh: Mini Review: Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy (Switch 2) - Pleasant But Perplexingly Piecemeal
articles.content_orig:
The latest addition to the pantheon of obscenely long-titled Nintendo Switch 2 Editions is a strange one. Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy takes the Switch 1 game that I have long considered ripe for a new hardware touch-up and does...not a lot with it. It's a chance to revisit one of Nintendo's finest games from the last generation, and the upgrade's price of admission (£7.99 / $9.99) is admittedly a small one, but on the 'new' front, I'm left wanting more.
Let's start with the usual 'Switch 2 Edition' bells and whistles. Pikmin 4 now plays in stunning native 4K resolution docked, and there's added GameShare support for those who want to play some cross-console Dandori Battles with a pal.
If you ask me, Pikmin 4 was already one of the best-looking titles on Switch 1, and the resolution bump doesn't feel transformative. That said, there's no denying that it's even more of a looker on the newer hardware.

articles.title_orig: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title_orig: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
articles.title_zh: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
articles.content_orig:
Amazon 's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.
The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.
At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights.
"If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."
The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.
Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google .
Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns , primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety , which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers.
Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam , in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.
The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot , which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.
Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot."
Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.
Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.
"People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said.
Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording.
Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot.
"We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside."
The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

articles.title_orig: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.title_zh: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.content_orig:
Ford Motor vehicles are displayed for sale at the Leif Johnson Ford dealership on June 30 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.
That's about $500 above the last record , set in December 2025.
Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.
Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly .
While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.
"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.
The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.
It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds , a car analytics company.
Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.
"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.
The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.
It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive . Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.
Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.
That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.
But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.
No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.
A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.
The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.
"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.
But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.
American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.
Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.
For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.
Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."
"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."
Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.
And the market for car buyers is smaller . About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.
Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."
For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

articles.title_orig: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.title_zh: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.content_orig:
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104.  Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.
After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of Ruillé-sur-Loir.
With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.
"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.
Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France,  Solange Alexandre, née Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.
"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917.   The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.
In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany.  She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.
"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.
Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's – a Tunisian-born French army veteran called Saïd Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.
Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.
"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.
In 1943 she met her first husband Guy Déliot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.
The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.
Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy.  There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.
"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.
After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).
Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.
Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the Légion d'Honneur , saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.
Finally in 2024 she relented.
On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour.  I am very proud – even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

articles.title_orig: FDA orders new warning labels on Ozempic, Wegovy over rare risk of permanent vision loss
articles.title_zh: FDA orders new warning labels on Ozempic, Wegovy over rare risk of permanent vision loss
articles.content_orig:
Apothecary Pharma recalls compounded tirzepatide vials distributed nationwide due to sterility concerns. Ashley Webster reports on the FDA classification of the recall and the North Carolina company's production practices.
The Food and Drug Administration has warned that those who take popular weight-loss drugs carry a small risk of developing a side effect that could lead to permanent vision loss .
The agency has instructed all GLP-1 drugmakers to affix new warning labels to their products, which treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The FDA's advisory applies to a dozen pill-based and injectable drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy.
The eye condition, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The condition, which has been reported in patients taking all GLP-1 drugs , occurs when blood flow to the optic nerve is reduced, though its underlying cause remains unclear, according to the FDA.
FDA scientists began investigating in 2024 after a study found that some patients taking semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic, experienced this type of vision loss. The FDA reviewed 126 clinical trials with 134,253 patients.
A package of Ozempic held by a customs officer in Hamburg, Germany, on April 17, 2025. (Marcus Brandt/picture alliance via Getty Images / Getty Images)
MAN CLAIMS HE WENT BLIND AFTER TAKING OZEMPIC, SHARES WARNING FOR OTHER USERS
The meta-analysis found that roughly six cases of the eye condition occurred per 100,000 patients taking GLP-1 drugs over a one-year period, compared with fewer than four cases among patients receiving a placebo or other glucose-lowering medications.
Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a roughly 68% higher rate of developing the eye condition, though the FDA cautioned that the findings do not establish a causal link.
Risk factors for the condition include diabetes, high blood pressure and sleep apnea , which are also common among patients prescribed GLP-1 drugs.
The FDA acknowledged that this overlap made it difficult to determine whether the medications themselves were responsible for the increased incidence of vision loss.
Wegovy injection pens arranged in Waterbury, Vermont, on Monday, April 28, 2025. (Shelby Knowles/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Of the roughly 78,000 patients included in the studies reviewed by the FDA, just 10 experienced vision loss, representing approximately 0.01% of participants.
Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is a rare condition that can cause permanent vision loss, with no proven treatment to reverse the damage.
A woman injecting a syringe of weight-loss medication into her stomach. (David Petrus Ibars/Getty Images / Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The condition is most common in adults over 50, who often experience sudden, painless vision loss in one eye upon waking. Symptoms include blurred vision, distorted color perception and blind spots.
However, research has found that approximately 43% of patients with significant vision impairment experience some spontaneous improvement, though visual field defects often persist.

articles.title_orig: Canada Signs New Deals With China After Trump Drops Trade Demand
articles.title_zh: Canada Signs New Deals With China After Trump Drops Trade Demand
articles.content_orig:
Canada has signed new economic agreements with China as Ottawa seeks to ease trade tensions with Washington.
Announced late on Monday following talks in Vancouver , the agreements deepen financial cooperation between Canada and China as Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to head to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu hosted He Lifeng, vice-premier of China, in Vancouver for negotiations.
Champagne said: “As two major economies with significant commercial ties, Canada and China share an interest in maintaining an open dialogue and advancing economic cooperation.
“Our discussions in Vancouver focused on opportunities to expand two-way trade and investment and deepen financial cooperation.
“By working together where our interest aligns, we can create new opportunities for Canadian businesses and workers and build a stronger, more resilient Canadian economy.”
Both countries have also agreed to extend an existing trade deal until the end of 2028. China will continue charging lower tariffs on Canadian products, including canola meal, peas, lobster and crab.
In return, Canada will continue allowing certain Chinese steel and aluminum products into the country without additional tariffs.
The deal is designed to help Canadian farmers and seafood businesses sell more products to China while giving Canadian companies access to Chinese metals they cannot easily buy at home.
The agreement also comes as Canada seeks to diversify its trade relationships amid continuing tariff disputes with the United States.
Carney said Washington had withdrawn a proposal that would have given the United States final approval over Canadian trade agreements with other countries.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has said a deal with Canada is close , but significant differences remain between the neighboring countries.
The discussions produced three agreements covering cooperation between the countries' finance ministries, financial regulators and central banks.
The arrangements establish closer dialogue on economic policy, cooperation between financial regulators and a joint working group involving the two countries' central banks.
Both sides also welcomed progress on a bilateral currency-swap arrangement and agreed to pursue greater financial-services market access.
The meetings followed Carney's January visit to Beijing , when he and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced a renewed strategic partnership.
The agreements form part of Carney's efforts to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States by expanding trade with other countries.
Speaking at a press conference, asked whether the new deal could jeopardize Canada’s trading relationship with the United States, Champagne said: “I would say every G7 country has a strategic relationship with China.
“Canada is no different in the sense that if one of the pillars is to diversify our trade, I would say it’s kind of obvious you have to talk to your second largest trading partner, which happens to be the second largest economy in the world.
“So I would say it goes without saying that Canada has strategic dialogue with China. You know, we are engaging. It’s very clear what are the guard rails.”
Philippe Rheault, director of the China Institute at the University of Alberta, who attended a reception with the Canadian finance minister and the Chinese and Canadian delegations in Vancouver, said: “My read of both ministers’ remarks is that the Canadian government is clearly signaling its plans to continue to lean in on broadened engagement with China, notwithstanding recent political developments in Washington.”
Meanwhile, the extension builds on an agreement reached during Carney's visit to Beijing in January, which helped ease a trade dispute that had hit Canadian agricultural exports.
China suspended a 100 percent tariff on Canadian canola meal in March, allowing it to enter the country duty-free. However, restrictions have not disappeared entirely: Canadian canola seed still faces a 14.9 percent tariff, while canola oil remains subject to a 100 percent duty.
The easing of restrictions has already coincided with a sharp increase in Canadian exports.
Canadian canola meal exports to China more than doubled from $104 million to $277 million, while pea exports rose from $76 million to $245 million. Lobster exports also increased by 57 percent, from $91 million to $142 million.
The wider arrangement supported industries sustaining more than 600,000 Canadian jobs.
China is already Canada's second-largest single-country merchandise trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $89 billion last year.
According to the latest figures from Ottawa’s Department of Finance, Canadian exports to China totaled $25 billion last year, while imports from China reached $64 billion.
Ottawa says Canadian merchandise exports to China have risen 41 percent so far in 2026 compared with the equivalent period last year.
Carney’s administration wants to increase exports to China by another 50 percent by 2030.
Trade negotiations with Washington and Ottawa remain ongoing but Newsweek understands both parties remain apart on a deal being reached.
A Canadian government official told Newsweek : “Progress is being made slowly, but there is still a way to go before we see any deal.”
Last week, Washington withdrew a demand that would have allowed the United States to exercise final approval over Canada's trade agreements with other countries alongside other demands for language and culture.
But tariffs on lumber, steel, aluminum and automobiles remain central sources of tension in the trading relationship.
Citing the tariffs, Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand says Ottawa will seek to ease trade frictions following Republican losses in the midterm elections.
Speaking at the Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers meeting in Paris, France, she said: “We’re talking about just a week or so out of these elections, and Canada very much hopes that we will have progress on the trade front.
“These sectors [lumber, steel, aluminum and automobiles] are being hit very hard in Canada, with workers losing their jobs.”
She said Canada has signed more than 20 security, economic and defense agreements over the past year, making Canada the only G7 nation to have a free trade agreement with each member of the group of advanced economies.
“This is the work that we are doing to double non-U.S. trade over the next 10 years,” she said.
Canada has also announced changes to its tariffs on American goods, extending relief for some US imports while preparing to reimpose duties on products that can be manufactured domestically.
Ottawa announced on November 9 that the country's tariff relief program would be extended until June 30, 2028.
The program allows Canadian businesses to avoid certain retaliatory tariffs on American products that are difficult to source in Canada.
The exemptions will also cover additional non-steel goods used in mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction, as well as products used by public education organizations.
However, Ottawa is withdrawing exemptions for some American goods where Canadian alternatives are available.
Certain U.S.-made trailers will lose relief from December 1, while specified aluminum wire, extrusions and paperboard products will become subject to tariffs again from February 1, 2027.
The changes are intended to protect Canadian manufacturers while limiting costs for businesses that depend on American supplies.
Canada has assessed $10 billion in tariffs on American goods between March 2025 and October 26, 2026.
Of that amount, approximately $6.30 billion had been relieved or omitted, leaving $3.7 billion in net tariff revenue.

articles.title_orig: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
articles.title_zh: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
articles.content_orig:
Affordability challenges are pushing some buyers out of the new vehicle market. Many are choosing used cars instead.
In turn, automakers are looking for ways to compete with many of the online retailers grabbing market share in the used car market and trying to bring some of those customers back into a new vehicle.
New vehicle sales tend to be more profitable for automakers, but reselling trade-ins as used vehicles is highly profitable for dealers. Used car prices are relatively strong, but newer online retailers such as Carvana and CarMax have made the market more competitive for dealers and other incumbent used car sellers.
"The internet and technology and apps on our phone have changed every aspect of retail, and probably one of the slowest areas of retail to have adopted to online and digital shopping has been the auto industry," said Ivan Feinseth, partner, chief investment officer and director of research at Tigress Financial Partners.
General Motors is a key example of automakers' attempts to address this shifting market. The automaker has revamped its certified used vehicle program, which now operates under the CarBravo name. It's essentially an online portal through which Chevrolet, Buick and GMC dealers can list their certified used vehicles and make them available to customers all over the U.S.
About 1,615 of GM's 3,700 dealers are enrolled in the program, according to the company. The only GM brand not involved is Cadillac, which maintains its own program.
"Certified" used or "preowned" vehicles are used cars that have undergone a thorough inspection and reconditioning. They typically come with guarantees and warranties from the manufacturer.
Many automakers have certified used programs for their own cars. But GM, as part of its revamp, is using CarBravo to certify vehicles made by other automakers. A lot of those cars arrive at dealerships as trade-ins, and often dealers will sell them to wholesale auctions, said John Fitzpatrick, senior manager of the CarBravo program.
"Wholesaling doesn't bring nearly the revenue that selling it to a new customer does," he said.
GM has said it is planning to net about 250,000 sales in its CarBravo program in 2026. Fitzpatrick said he doesn't expect that even half of those will end up being new car sales.
But through CarBravo, the customer gets access to GM's dealership network for service, something Fitzpatrick says is a key differentiator between its program and growing online sellers. CarBravo vehicles come with various warranties, depending on the age and mileage on the car.
GM said the program is driving more traffic into local dealerships, where purchases are typically finalized. That creates an opportunity to convert a used car shopper into a new car buyer. So far, the automaker said about 38% of the shoppers initially looking for used cars end up buying new.
A customer who wants to buy a full-size truck can look on the website and compare used Chevrolet Silverados alongside used Ford F-150s and Ram 1500s, for example. The buyer might settle on a used truck from any of those brands, but a conversation with a dealer can push them in a different direction.
"The customer picks up the phone, but in the back of their mind, they maybe always have been a traditional, more new car customer," Fitzpatrick said.
"You've shown the customer, you're going to pay $500 [per month] for this used F-150, but you may pay $510 or $515 for this new Chevy," he said. "And now all of a sudden the customer says, yeah, maybe I can do that because I'd rather have that new vehicle than the used truck."
While the average transaction price of a new vehicle is about $50,000, the average 3-year-old used car costs about $30,000 as of September, according to Cox Automotive.
However, industry analysts say customers base their purchasing decisions on the cost of the monthly payment more than on the sticker price of the car.
New cars often come with longer-term loan options than used ones, Feinseth said, which can result in lower monthly payments.
"On a 1- or 2-year-old car, you may be only stuck with a 3- or 4-year loan," he said. "On a new car, you can get a 5-year, 6-year loan."
The share of new car loans lasting 84 months hit a new record in the third quarter, at more than 1 in 4 loans, according to Edmunds.
Meanwhile, used car prices in some affordable segments have risen, according to Cox Automotive, and about three quarters of consumers express some interest in certified cars.
But the key is building the relationship with the customer, he said. About 50% of the buyers GM has gained through the program appear to be new to the brand, meaning there is no record of them in any of the automaker's customer databases. About 70% had never visited the dealership they ended up purchasing from.
"The goal is really to get that customer engaged with the store, give them the option of building a relationship with the dealer," he said. "The dealer can really help the customer figure out what works for their budget."
It's a boon for dealers too: Customers buying warranty-backed used cars often return to the dealership for service visits — which often account for about half of a dealership's profits. GM can also sell subscriptions to connected vehicle services, such as its OnStar, which provides safety, security and navigation services.
"That is a big part of General Motors' business going forward, is to sell the software and subscription services like OnStar and eventually to the cars that are enabled with Super Cruise," GM's advanced driver-assistance system, Feinseth said.
GM isn't the only automaker trying to use its certified preowned vehicle program to lure buyers.
Detroit rival Ford Motor also certifies vehicles made by other manufacturers through its Ford Blue Advantage program. It is on track to do 450,000 total sales in 2026, more than GM's 250,000 target. It didn't specify how many of those buyers end up purchasing new vehicles.
Toyota told CNBC in an email that about 40% of its used car shoppers end up buying new instead.
Honda didn't give specifics about its program. But Lance Woelfer, American Honda's vice president of automobile sales, said conversions happen "probably every day at dealerships throughout the country."
"But it also is more about that first interaction with the consumer," Woelfer said. "And there are people in any market that prefer to buy a used vehicle, but appreciate the confidence that a [certified preowned designation] can give them."
Woelfer said those customers come back to get their vehicles serviced at a rate about 18% higher than someone who buys a non-certified used car. They also return to purchase a new car at a rate about 7% to 8% higher in the future, he said.
"It's about that first relationship that allows us to then have that customer loyalty for life," he added. "And that's where our focus is. We've been doing it a long time, and we've seen a lot of benefits from the certified business."
