articles.title_orig: Iran lifts 2,000km limit on its ballistic missiles: What that means
articles.title_zh: Iran lifts 2,000km limit on its ballistic missiles: What that means
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has lifted its self-imposed 2,000km (1,250-mile) limit on the range of its ballistic missiles, raising questions over whether Tehran now considers hitting targets beyond the Middle East.
“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi announced at a news conference in Tehran on Saturday.
Mohebbi did not say whether Iran already had missiles that exceed the cap, but added that Iran would show its capabilities through action rather than statements, as Tehran has hardened its position and shifted towards an “offensive” military doctrine.
The announcement came days after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that “any kind and level of threat” from the United States or Israel would be met with a response unlimited by geography. Mojtaba has said Iran needs to end the “no war, no peace” situation amid the volatile status of the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade on the Iranian ports.
It also comes as the diplomatic push to end the US-Israel war on Iran has intensified, with Trump on Monday saying there is “positive momentum” towards ending the military hostilities after talks with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani in Washington, DC.
So what does lifting the limit actually change, and why is Iran doing it now?
Iran already has operational capabilities to launch missiles beyond 2,000km, but it has kept a cap on them amid focus on regional deterrence. Iranian missiles can reach the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt, as well as parts of Southeastern Europe, including Greece, Bulgaria, Romania, Albania, North Macedonia and Serbia.
For Gulf states, the announcement changes little. They already sit well within Iran’s 2,000km range and have come under repeated Iranian missile fire since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28.
The change can help Iran to position some of its rocket launchers in the country’s east, from where it would require a bigger range to reach Israel. The US and its European allies fear Iran can target US bases in the Indian Ocean and Europe.
In March, the United Kingdom accused Iran of firing missiles towards the joint US-UK base at Diego Garcia, some 4,000km (about 2,500 miles) from Iran. Tehran denied targeting the base located in the Indian Ocean, saying it was “ an Israeli false flag ” operation.
In 2019, the UK, France and Germany said their modelling put a lighter-warhead version of Iran’s Khorramshahr missile at a range of approximately 3,000km (about 1,900 miles). US officials have also said technology from Iran’s space programme could be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles, The Associated Press news agency reported. Iran currently does not have intercontinental ballistic missiles in its arsenal.
Muhanad Seloom, assistant professor of international politics and security at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Diego Garcia launch had already made Iran’s point. “Iran denied doing that, but they wanted to signal that they have the capacity. So yes, they do have the capacity,” he said.
Seloom, who is also an honorary research fellow at the University of Exeter, pointed to Iran’s space launches over the past decade, saying the same rockets could in theory reach anywhere in the world. “How effective, that’s a totally different story,” he said, adding that Iran could probably field missiles with a range of about 5,000km (3,100 miles).
Iranian security analyst Mohamed Taheri made a similar case on Iran’s state-run Channel 3, saying range had stopped being a technical obstacle for Iran by the mid-2010s. “Even now we have no technical limitation in reaching ranges above 2,000km,” he said.
“If we were to increase that range to 4,000km, we would certainly have most of Europe within our missile range, and roughly most of North Africa as well,” Taheri said.
The IRGC announcement about ending its self-imposed limit seems to be a shift from Tehran’s assurances to Europe on missile range. Europe’s relations with Iran have deteriorated over its nuclear programme and regional geopolitical ambitions. The European Union’s designation of the IRGC as a “terrorist” group and its allowing the US to use bases on the continent have attracted Iran’s ire.
Iran warned Bulgaria repeatedly this year over US aircraft on its soil. In April, Tehran sent a diplomatic note cautioning Bulgaria against letting US military aircraft use its airports for operations against Iran.
When Bulgaria’s parliament approved hosting up to eight US KC-135 refuelling tankers at Bezmer airbase in July, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Bulgarian decision-makers “must bear responsibility” for the move. It was Tehran’s third warning to Sofia.
In August, two Iranian insiders told the Financial Times that the US bases in countries such as Bulgaria had been assessed as possible targets, describing the threat to Europe as real but confined to the continent’s south and southeast. Two US tankers left Bezmer on August 21.
Last month, the UK spy chief said Iran is stepping up targeting of military bases in Europe. It came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the IRGC was “almost certainly” behind a suspected plot against Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, an airbase used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. The incident prompted the US to withdraw its military jets from the facility over security concerns earlier this month. Tehran has denied involvement, saying it was a “false flag” operation.
On Monday, the US military evacuated aircraft from a second British base, RAF Mildenhall, “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, according to The Wall Street Journal. The refuelling tankers were moved to Germany and elsewhere, and US officials were still discussing the precise nature of the threat.
The UK Ministry of Defence did not confirm the reason. “Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” a spokesperson said.
Bases in the UK, Germany and Romania are among other European locations the US has used during the conflict.
“It’s possible that in this war we may set aside the geographic restraint we’ve observed stemming from our diplomatic relations with certain countries and even be able to strike the bases that exist in Europe,” Iran’s Taheri said.
For European governments, the announcement is “worrying … but not alarming”, Doha Institute’s Seloom said. Missiles would have to travel far to reach mainland Europe or the UK, he explained, giving NATO members with assets in the region early warning and time to intercept them.
He said threatening Europe would not serve Iran’s interests, since European governments did not back Trump’s war and have pushed for a diplomatic solution despite paying a heavy price in energy costs. That could change if Iran comes to be framed as a threat to international security, he warned, pointing to Iraq, where successive UN Security Council resolutions preceded European support for the 2003 invasion.
“No one could defend Iranian policies when it comes to threatening Europe or the UK,” Seloom said. Lifting the limit, he added, suggests Tehran “is reading this conflict as existential now”.
That, he argued, is what should concern the whole region. “When you give them the idea that you have only one option, is to die … they can do anything. There would be no red lines,” he said.
Because the cap was self-imposed, Iran could have dropped it at any time. For years, the IRGC said the limit was meant to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.
Mohebbi, the IRGC spokesman, went further, saying that if Iran decided to change its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations would be made .

articles.title_orig: Khazalite Holds make their Battle Report debut
articles.title_zh: Khazalite Holds make their Battle Report debut
articles.content_orig:
Khazalite Holds make their Battle Report debut
The final cut of Blacktalon launches on Warhammer TV this week! It’s more than three and a half hours of action-packed animation following Sigmar’s legendary hunter.
And before that, there’s the debut of Khazalite Holds on Battle Report and exclusive interviews with author Robert Rath and Golden Demon legend Albert Moreto Font. Let’s dig in…
The forces of the Khazalite Holds make their Battle Report debut in a bitter clash against their fallen kin – the Helsmiths of Hashut. Can guest player Jay, from the Warhammer Studio, overcome the followers of the Bullfather in an epic 2,000 point bout?
Since this is the first time that the Khazalite Holds have done battle on Warhammer TV, we thought it might be good to share Jay’s army list to give some ideas of how to blend together Grimmdron (or Fyreslayers as you might still know them) and Kromdron.
Battle Formation: Hearthsworn Defenders Heroic Trait: Innate Resonance Artefact of Power: Deep-earth Runic Weapon Spell Lore: Reverberations of the Runes Manifestation Lore: Aetherwrought Machineries Runefather on Magmadroth Runeson on Magmadroth 5 Auric Hearthguard 9 Vulkyn Flameseekers Hjulda Drakkblud Thrynn 10 Clanshields 10 Clanshields Runewright Oathkeeper Cannon Stonebreaker Mortar 3 Gholems of Gazul
Jay went with the Hearthsworn Defenders battle formation, giving his force access to the Lock Shields! ability, making them particularly durable against enemy shooting when defending their home territory or a crucial objective.
Dug in and resolute, little can pierce the well-made defences of these duardin.
Effect: Subtract 1 from hit rolls for shooting attacks that target friendly KHAZALITE HOLDS units while they are wholly within friendly territory or while every model in the unit is contesting an objective you control.
We sat down with Battle Report host Si (who commanded the Helsmiths of Hashut) to learn what it was like to face the newest faction in Warhammer Age of Sigmar.
Warhammer Community: What were your first impressions of fighting against the Khazalite Holds?
Si: Don’t expect to outshoot them! Even without any Clangunners, Jay’s artillery – he had an Oathkeeper Cannon and a Stonebreaker Mortar – was a constant menace to my army, while the accuracy of my own ranged units was hampered by his Locked Shields. What was worse, after winning priority in the first battle round, Jay moved aggressively to secure the forward objectives and thereby expand the battle formation’s area of effect beyond his territory. I mean, a Deathshrieker Rocket Battery can hit with truly devastating force, but when it’s reduced to hitting on a 5+, it’s far less reliable.
WarCom: In many ways the Helsmiths of Hashut are a dark mirror of the Khazalite Holds – how do they compare as armies?
Si: Aside from the more obvious nuances that their respective faction rules offer, I would say that the key differences lie in speed in the case of the Helsmiths versus the even heavier armour of the Kromdron units in particular. Okay, so Helmsmiths are far from the fastest faction, but their access to hard-hitting cavalry units in the form of Anointed Sentinels and Bull Centaurs gives them an edge over their bipedal cousins, while their Infernal Taurus-riding Daemonsmiths can Fly, unlike the Khazalites on War Thrones or Magmadroths. Of course, the Khazalites make up for this relative shortfall* with an overwhelming number of 3+ Save characteristics as well as multiple ways to mitigate the effectiveness of incoming attacks.
WarCom: Are there any particular Khazalite Holds combinations that opponents need to keep an eye out for?
Si: At first glance, it would be easy to overlook the potential of Clanshields . However, pair them up with a Thrynn, or better still, Hjulda Drakkblud, and they can become a real force to be reckoned with. Under the right circumstances, you can improve four of the five characteristics of their Kromdron Weapons without the use of any command abilities, all the while reducing the Rend of incoming attacks and ignoring the first damage point they suffer in each phase. Underestimate them at your peril!
WarCom: Do you have any tips for players wanting to defeat the Khazalites?
Si: Well, as I mentioned earlier, they’re tough opponents to outshoot, so you really need to take the fight to them if you want to avoid being shot to pieces. That being said, breaking through the Khazalite lines to counter their artillery and powerful ranged units is easier said than done. This is where abilities that enable you to instantly relocate across the battlefield or otherwise break through their lines can come in clutch. Judicious use of pile-ins or a well-timed Power Through, for example, may help you to bog down a key ranged unit before they can shoot you in the following turn.**
WarCom: Finally, do you have a favourite unit from the new battletome?
Si: Hmm… It would be easy to say High Kyng Valankrom, as he’s not only a magnificent model (or should that be diorama?), but he’s a real force multiplier, and rock-solid in a fight. That being said, I think I’d actually have to say the humble Clanshields. I don’t think I would leave the hold without two reinforced units of 20 to form the backbone of my Khazalite throng.
Thanks, Si! Tune in to see if the infernal sorcery of Daemonsmith Urak Taar is enough to hold back the tide of vengeance that seeks to smash his forces, and don’t forget that the new Khazalite Holds miniatures are available to pre-order now .
Robert Rath, author of fan-favourite novel The Infinite and the Divine is the guest on Scribes and Scriveners , talking about his latest novel, The Wicked and the Warped . The sequel sees Orikan the Diviner and Trazyn the Infinite thrown into an unlikely alliance to uncover the secrets of a rediscovered world from ancient Necron history.
Presenter Alex talks to Robert about his latest novel and what exactly this means for Orikan and Trazyn’s relationship – can they finally set aside their differences or are they doomed to an eternity of petty bickering?
This week on Painting Desk , presenter Ed is joined by multiple Slayer Sword winner Albert Moreto Font . Albert talks about his painting journey, how he made his start in Warhammer, and how he has managed to stay passionate and motivated throughout years of competitions. He also gives a unique insight into the world of competition painting, the importance of the wider community, and even dispels a few myths around Golden Demon .
Watch the complete animated adventures of Sigmar’s foremost assassin, as all 12 episodes of Blacktalon are brought together into a single action-packed feature-length epic. We’ll have more on this huge supercut here on Warhammer Community on Friday.
This week’s features join an incredible back catalogue of over 700 episodes including original animations, hobby guides and gaming content. If you subscribe for an entire year, you’ll also gain automatic entry into regular competitions, a copy of the Warhammer Yearbook and even a pair of special subscriber-only miniatures. If that wasn’t enough, an annual subscription nets you 12 months of content for the price of 9.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia Sentences Mother to 100 Lashes for Birth Outside Marriage
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia Sentences Mother to 100 Lashes for Birth Outside Marriage
articles.content_orig:
By IMOGEN GARFINKEL - SENIOR FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 10:05 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 10:10 EST, 10 November 2026
Saudi Arabia has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes after she gave birth outside of marriage.
The sentence is a crushing blow to the mother, who has attempted for more than a year to return to Kenya with her child but has been blocked at every turn.
The ruling, issued last month, shows the limits of a decade of social and legal reforms in the kingdom, where women can be jailed for 'illegal pregnancy'.
The mother of five, Esther Wanja Muthoni, is among thousands of East African domestic workers who were recruited as housekeepers and nannies in Saudi Arabia.
But if they become pregnant, the women end up trapped in a bureaucratic maze, a New York Times investigation last year revealed.
Not only that, but they are exposed to violence. Hundreds of Kenyan women have been killed, while reports of rape and beatings are common, the newspaper claimed.
For women who become pregnant, like Ms. Muthoni, giving birth brings added punishment and danger.
'I am so afraid,' Ms. Muthoni, 40, told the newspaper in a phone interview last month. 'I don’t think I can endure those lashes.' Under Saudi law, women are seated and clothed while lashed across the body with a bamboo stick.
Saudi Arabia has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes after she gave birth outside of marriage
'I don’t deserve this,' she said of the lashings in a recent interview.
The children of unwed mothers are regularly denied birth certificates and Kenya's diplomats, responsible for issuing them and helping mothers and children get home, frequently ignore them, insult them and solicit bribes for sex.
Ms. Muthoni and her 1-year-old son, Abudy, are victims of an exploitative industry that recruits African women to Saudi Arabia in a labour pipeline from which top Kenyan government officials profit, the newspaper alleged.
The woman was working legally as a domestic worker through Maharah Human Resources, a Saudi corporation, when she had a brief relationship with an Egyptian resident of the kingdom and became pregnant.
After she gave birth in August 2025 in staff housing, a supervisor discovered them and took her to hospital.
There, police officers detained her for questioning about the pregnancy.
According to statements given to the police, Ms. Muthoni said that the father, a man named Mohamud, had left the country.
She was released but was subsequently refused entry from staff accommodation and a shelter.
She also received no help from the Kenyan Embassy.
Ms. Muthoni started living at a petrol station that had become a meeting place for migrant mothers, many of whom craved deportation with their children.
Last year, Maharah provided her with somewhere to stay and the Kenyan Embassy provided documents permitting her to depart the country.
But she could not depart from Saudi Arabia while the legal case against her was pending.
Multiple hearings took place last summer before a three-judge panel at a criminal court in Riyadh, according to court documents.
Ms. Muthoni says she had been provided with a court translator but not a lawyer.
While indigent defendants in Saudi criminal cases are entitled to state-sponsored lawyers, trials often proceed without them in practice, even in some capital cases, according to experts.
Sex and pregnancy outside of marriage are effectively in a legally grey area, where some women face no repercussions and others are prosecuted.
The legal system of the country is grounded in Sharia, or Islamic law.
Because the kingdom lacks a written penal code, judges interpret Islamic law on a case-by-case basis.
A court found Ms. Muthoni guilty of having sex before marriage in October.
The verdict was delivered after judges relied on an orthodox interpretation of Islamic law that prescribes 100 lashes based on a verse in the Quran.
The court judgment does not suggest that the state pursued the father.
'This sentence of flogging does not align with international human rights standards,'  Ekaterina Porras Sivolobova, a labour migration analyst and founder of the nonprofit Do Bold, told the New York Times.
She added: 'It strips a mother of her dignity and does the opposite of protecting vulnerable women. It targets them.'
In 2020, the government announced significant curbs to the sentence of lashes, but Ms. Muthoni's situation shows inconsistencies in the kingdom's supposed reforms.
At the time of the government move six years ago, state-owned media described the announcement as a 'landmark decision'.
While Saudi and international news outlets gave the impression that flogging had been abolished, the decision left a loophole for cases in which Islamic law prescribes flogging, including for sex outside marriage.
It is impossible to determine how often lashing is still ordered, because judgements for morality crimes are not routinely published.
Without any legal representation, Ms. Muthoni did not appeal her sentence.
'It is the only way that can take me back home to my children,' she said.
Following the ruling issued last month, it is unclear when the lashing will take place.
The Kenyan exit documents have also expired, so it is not clear whether or how she and her son will be allowed to return to Kenya.
As well as the lashes, the court sentenced Ms. Muthoni to a year of banishment.
Under Saudi law, if a judgment does not specify a destination, the person is usually sent to another Saudi city.
Courts are able to review such sentences if women have no male relatives to accompany them.
It was not known whether this means Ms. Muthoni will be deported to Kenya.

articles.title_orig: Rocket Lab Backlog Went to the Moon. The Stock Is Down Anyway.
articles.title_zh: Rocket Lab Backlog Went to the Moon. The Stock Is Down Anyway.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Rocket Lab (RKLB) sank 8% as a wider loss and thinner margins overshadowed record $4 billion backlog, while AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) slid 4%.
Rocket Lab's Iridium (IRDM) deal drove one-time costs, while AST SpaceMobile's $1 billion-plus Firefly (FLY) engine deal fuels its homegrown Blacklift rocket ambitions.
Peter Beck calls launch capacity "extremely constrained," with Neutron's first 16 flights booked, tying Rocket Lab, AST SpaceMobile and SpaceX together.
Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)
Space stocks are falling as the market processes two quarterly reports that landed after the November 9 close. Rocket Lab ( NASDAQ:RKLB ) stock is at $53.33, down 9% in morning trading. The company's Q3 2026 report combined a record backlog with a wider-than-expected loss, and the selloff shows which half of that story is carrying more weight.
AST SpaceMobile ( NASDAQ:ASTS ) is also lower after Bank of America ( NYSE:BAC ) Securities cut its price target on the stock. SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ) is falling too. Launch capacity ties the three together, since Rocket Lab sells it, AST SpaceMobile needs it and SpaceX dominates it.
Rocket Lab disclosed on November 9 that Q3 revenue reached $267.83 million, up 72.7% year over year and ahead of the $257.18 million consensus. The company's loss under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) was $0.12 per share, missing expectations for a $0.0665 loss. Two one-time items drove much of that miss: a $27.26 million loss on retiring convertible notes and $21.34 million in costs for the pending acquisition of Iridium Communications ( NASDAQ:IRDM ).

Other details likely added pressure. Non-GAAP gross margin at Rocket Lab falling to 38.4% from 41.9% a year earlier. Neutron's first launch now sits no earlier than 2027, and Rocket Lab CFO Adam Spice said adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) should turn positive within six months of the rocket's first successful flight. Funding for Iridium came partly from new shares, as Rocket Lab's at-the-market program raised $2.4 billion in gross proceeds.
The bull case starts with demand. Backlog at Rocket Lab hit a record $3.57 billion. CEO Peter Beck stated on the call that "Neutron's first 16 launches are booked and the next available slots are in the 2030s." Several of those missions carry a new $70 million base price. Management's Q4 2026 revenue guidance of $270 million to $290 million sits above the $265.42 million consensus.
On November 10, the Pentagon offered Rocket Lab a $150 million conditional loan to speed up Neutron. Closing that commitment still requires Rocket Lab to meet financial, legal and due diligence requirements.
AST SpaceMobile stock is at $34.60, down 6%. Bank of America Securities cut its price target to $45 from $80 and kept a Neutral rating, citing a slower launch pace, later commercial availability and execution risk in AST SpaceMobile's plan to build its own rocket. The research note followed the company's Q3 report, in which revenue of $42.32 million missed the $46 million consensus while the loss of $0.44 per Class A share came in slightly better than the $0.4479 estimate. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance at AST SpaceMobile held at $150 million to $200 million.
By mid-2027, AST SpaceMobile targets about 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit, and it revealed Blacklift, a reusable rocket with first launches targeted for late 2028. Engines for Blacklift will come from Firefly Aerospace ( NASDAQ:FLY ) under a $1.3 billion supply agreement.
SpaceX stock is at $137.87, down 3%, a smaller decline than either Rocket Lab or AST SpaceMobile. That's a softer move for the sector's largest company, which last reported quarterly results on October 20.
Rocket Lab sells launch services and builds spacecraft for commercial, government and defense customers, and it's adding satellite communications through Iridium. On the call, Beck described launch capacity as extremely constrained, and when asked about AST SpaceMobile building its own rocket, he said Rocket Lab is rooting for everybody.
AST SpaceMobile partners with mobile network operators to deliver cellular broadband directly to standard smartphones, which makes the company a buyer of launch until Blacklift flies. A batch of its BlueBird satellites is already waiting on a SpaceX launch date.
SpaceX competes with Rocket Lab for launch contracts through its Falcon rockets and Starship, while its Starlink unit competes with AST SpaceMobile in direct-to-cell service. That dual role makes SpaceX both a supplier to AST SpaceMobile and a rival to it.
Rocket Lab now faces two questions: whether Neutron moves from tank testing to a firm launch date and whether the Iridium acquisition closes. A clean test campaign could support the case that the record backlog turns into revenue, while another delay could keep pressure on margins and cash flow.
AST SpaceMobile management noted on the call it will revealed Blacklift at an event in New York City on November 12. Traders can watch for a confirmed SpaceX launch date for the next BlueBird batch, given that Bank of America Securities cited launch pace as a risk, and execution risk on a homegrown rocket sits against maintained guidance and a growing list of government contracts.
Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile are both combined strong demand with heavy spending, which leaves each stock sensitive to every development milestone, and investors may want to research the timing of Neutron's first flight closely as that milestone resolves.

articles.title_orig: IDF prepares for surprise Iranian attack as US pursues deal with Tehran
articles.title_zh: IDF prepares for surprise Iranian attack as US pursues deal with Tehran
articles.content_orig:
The IDF is preparing for two major escalation scenarios involving Iran as the United States, steered by US Vice President JD Vance, continues diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement with Tehran and preventing a broader regional conflict.
The talks are focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restoring international nuclear inspections in exchange for partially lifting the US blockade on Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. Israeli defense officials remain on high alert as diplomatic efforts continue alongside limited US military strikes.
The first scenario the IDF has prepared for involves the United States launching an extensive and particularly aggressive military offensive against Iran, targeting national infrastructure and military facilities in an effort to shorten the conflict and bring it to an end.
The second scenario involves Iran attempting a surprise attack against American interests and military bases across the Middle East, including IDF bases hosting US military personnel and aircraft.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir and senior General Staff officers have held discussions and situational assessments in recent days to review and validate operational plans.
As a result of these discussions, Israel Air Force Commander Maj.-Gen. Omer Tishler and Operations Directorate head Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen did not attend the IDF Commanders' Championship.
The assessments cover a wide range of scenarios and potential responses, aimed at ensuring operational readiness in the event of a surprise Iranian attack.
The military is also preparing for the possibility that Israel's adversaries in its immediate and wider regional surroundings could become involved in an escalation, whether through a coordinated operation, misunderstanding, or miscalculation.
Meanwhile, Israeli defense officials assess that US President Donald Trump would prefer to avoid a military confrontation and resolve tensions through a diplomatic agreement.
However, Israeli security assessments suggest that the Iranian leadership views Washington's preference for diplomacy as a sign of weakness.
According to these assessments, Tehran views the results of the US midterm elections , held on Tuesday, November 3, as a form of political "revenge" against the White House.
Israeli officials also believe Iran is unlikely to rush into signing an agreement and will instead maintain a hard-line negotiating position while attempting to prolong the talks.
In recent days, US forces have carried out limited strikes against Iranian military assets in the south of the country and around the Strait of Hormuz, including operations targeting air defense systems and missile launchers on Qeshm Island.
Additional reported operations have targeted Iranian military positions on Larak Island, while Iranian forces have retaliated against American military assets and vessels in the region. The timing and full extent of all the reported strikes have not been independently confirmed.
The military developments have unfolded alongside ongoing diplomatic contacts, highlighting the risk that limited exchanges could escalate despite efforts to reach an agreement.
Separately, Israeli defense officials addressed discussions held on November 1, two days before the US midterm elections, during which senior security officials reviewed potential scenarios and responses involving Iran.
Among the options raised was the possibility of a preemptive Israeli offensive against Iran, reportedly supported by the Mossad chief.
However, security officials said they considered the proposal and then dropped it, rejecting suggestions that the discussions involved unusually heated disagreements.
"The option was raised and then dropped just as quickly," security officials said. "The discussion was professional and respectful. There were disagreements on some issues, but no arguments that got out of proportion."
"The leaks from the discussion were politically motivated," the officials added.

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. They would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped up security.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.
Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to airbases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk.
It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain , RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike the Islamic Republic.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on this week’s movements and said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and remained under discussion by U.S. officials.
“We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News.
“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement,” a U.S. European Command official said. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets,” the European Command official added.
A spokesperson for the U.K.’s Ministry of Defense said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.”
“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said.
It comes weeks after the U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials previously told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at that base, located in Gloucestershire.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. Other arrests followed and two men were charged under the National Security Act.
The incident, which attracted huge international attention, remains largely unexplained although British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the activity was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
Though Tehran has denied involvement in any plot against RAF Fairford, its powerful Revolutionary Guard warned in July that any base used to launch attacks against Iranian territory was a legitimate target.
Iran has vowed retaliation for any renewal of the American-Israeli war against it and has threatened to expand its response beyond the Middle East.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington had addressed concerns around reported threats from Tehran against American diplomats overseas by “moving people away from the threat.”
“Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas,” Rubio said. “And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.”
Citing new “momentum” in negotiations to end the war, President Donald Trump on Monday downplayed the prospect of new U.S. attacks.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said following a meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani.
Further U.S. attacks “won’t be necessary” at this point, but Washington remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, Trump told reporters at the White House.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Matthew Mulligan is a senior reporter for the NBC News Social Newsgathering team based in London.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.title_zh: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.content_orig:
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
Netanyahu - Israel's longest-serving leader - reiterated in a video on Monday his call for the formation of a government of national unity, which he said he would lead as prime minister.
He said any Zionist party - those which support Israel as a Jewish state - including opposition parties, would be eligible. He warned against a government which relied on what he called "the Islamists", an apparent reference to Arab parties.
"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he said.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30%, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30%, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian drones struck the KINEF refinery in Russia's Leningrad region on Monday, causing major fires and damaging three oil processing units.
Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defences shot down 113 drones targeting the region, but debris from one struck the roof of a multi-storey building in Vsevolozhsk, killing a resident.
Three main processing units at the Kirishinefteorgsintez (KINEF) plant were damaged.
KINEF, the largest refinery in northwest Russia and second largest in the country behind the Omsk facility, is owned by the Surgutneftegaz group and processes roughly 18 million tonnes of crude oil a year, about 7% of Russia's total refining capacity.
The plant produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil, bitumen and petrochemical products, and supplies aviation fuel to St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport. Its design capacity is 20-21 million tonnes annually.
The refinery has been targeted multiple times by Ukrainian forces since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Surgutneftegaz was placed under EU, US and UK sanctions in 2025.
Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces shot down 430 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions and occupied Crimea overnight. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
Rosneft announced on Monday it was capping petrol and diesel sales at its filling stations. The restrictions took effect in Karelia, Buryatia, Zabaykalsky Krai, and the Novosibirsk, Arkhangelsk and Penza regions, according to Russian media.
In cities, customers are limited to 30 litres of petrol per transaction; on motorways, the cap is 50 litres. In Krasnoyarsk Krai, separate limits apply: 30 litres of AI-95, 50 litres of AI-92 and 100 litres of diesel per customer.
Authorities in Leningrad region also recommended filling stations cap petrol sales at 30 litres and diesel at 50 litres per transaction.
Russian forces launched 317 Shahed drones since Monday evening, including 105 jet-powered variants and Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and decoy drones, Ukraine's air force said. Of these, 276 were shot down. Impacts were recorded in 31 locations and falling debris in nine more.
A drone strike on a food warehouse in Odesa on Monday morning killed three people and left one in serious condition.
Two people were killed and seven injured in strikes on Dnipropetrovsk region. Nine people, including children, were injured in attacks on Kharkiv region overnight on Tuesday.
Six people, including one child, were wounded in strikes on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding area.
Seven people were injured in a drone strike on Kremenchuk in Poltava region, among them a 16-year-old. A rehabilitation centre for children with disabilities was destroyed in the attack.
In Sumy, three power workers were injured on Monday morning when a Russian strike hit their vehicle.
Russian forces struck rescue teams in Kamyshivakha three times with drones as they cleared rubble from a Russian air strike on 2 November that killed 55 people. Up to 19 may still be trapped under the debris. Police have identified 30 of the dead.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia’s vice-president ‘intends to resign’ after qualifications questioned
articles.title_zh: Indonesia’s vice-president ‘intends to resign’ after qualifications questioned
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, left, walks with President Prabowo Subianto after Subianto delivered his State of the Nation Address at the parliament building in Jakarta, Indonesia, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. Dita Alangkara/AP hide caption
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.
The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

articles.title_orig: China-CEEC forum calls for greater win-win cooperation
articles.title_zh: China-CEEC forum calls for greater win-win cooperation
articles.content_orig:
SOFIA — The 6th China-Central and Eastern Europe High-Level Think Tank Scholars Forum, themed "China-Europe Dialogue: Expanding Synergies and Embracing a Win-Win Future," was held on Monday, bringing together more than 100 experts and scholars from Bulgaria, Croatia, Romania, Serbia and other countries.
Wang Junwei, director of the Academic and Editorial Committee of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said in his keynote speech that seeking common ground while preserving differences and pursuing cooperation for mutual benefit are important principles guiding China's approach to international relations and valuable experience in ensuring the steady development of China-Europe relations. These principles will continue to play a guiding role in cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European countries (CEEC) in the future, he said.
In her welcome remarks, Chinese Ambassador to Bulgaria Dai Qingli said that as long as China and Europe uphold mutual respect and engage in equal-footed consultations, both sides will be able to find solutions to problems and continuously expand the scope for mutually beneficial cooperation.
Nataliya Kiselova, former president of the National Assembly of Bulgaria, said in her remarks that the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC demonstrated the CPC leadership's courage to uphold the truth and curb abuses of power, and its determination to continue consolidating its position as the core of leadership in Chinese society.
ALSO READ: China-CEEC cooperation opening doors
Wu Haitao, vice president of the China Public Diplomacy Association, said that think-tank exchanges serve as an important channel for continuously strengthening the public-opinion foundation of China-Europe friendship.
Participants held in-depth discussions on China's 15th Five-Year Plan, the four major global initiatives, global governance, and the prospects and vision for China-EU relations.
The inaugural forum was held in 2016. Since then, it has played an active role in facilitating exchanges of ideas and building consensus among think-tank scholars from China and CEEC.
READ MORE: China-CEEC business ties win-win for both
This year's forum was jointly organized by the Scientific Research Planning Department of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, the Chinese Embassy in Bulgaria, the China Public Diplomacy Association, the Bulgaria National Association for the Belt and Road, and Sofia University.

One scientist goes further, citing Nanzuo and Langzhou as proof of China’s unbroken 5,000-year history
The ancient palace would have been considered a crown jewel of its people. Foreigners would have admired it with awe, and locals would have held it in great esteem.
Then, 5,000 years ago, the villagers deliberately buried it, and we do not know why.
A team of scientists announced several updates in mid-October about their work at Nanzuo, an ancient capital city near Qingyang, Gansu, in northwest China. Most of the updates concerned a central palace that would have been the cultural hub of the region’s most important city at the time.

articles.title_zh: I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too
articles.content_orig:
By JO MACFARLANE, HEALTH REPORTER
Published: 02:01 EST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 05:58 EST, 26 October 2026
Sitting in the park with her grandchildren one afternoon, Becky Tucker decided to overhaul her life.
As the four of them played and ran around, Becky, then 48, simply lacked the energy to join in. It was, she says now, a wake-up call.
The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had been struggling with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes as perimenopause took hold.
And for as long as she could remember, she had experienced intense, debilitating migraines for a week every month, linked to her menstrual cycle.
She was also significantly overweight – something she had struggled with her whole life. At more than 13 stone and with a BMI of 29 – bordering on obese – Becky had spent the previous 25 years on various weight-loss plans.
They'd worked, to begin with, but then she piled on the pounds again when she returned to her usual diet of chocolate bars and what she calls 'beige stodge'.
It will be a familiar scenario to many in midlife – the pounds creep on until it no longer feels possible to shift them.
But three years on, it is no exaggeration to say that Becky is transformed. Indeed, as our photos show so clearly, she is almost unrecognisable. Fizzing with energy and an astonishing four stone lighter, she says she feels like a different woman.
Becky Tucker shed four stone by following the ZOE diet. The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had  previously struggled with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes
At more than 13 stone and with a BMI of 29 – bordering on obese – Becky had spent the previous 25 years on various weight-loss plans
Previous diets worked, but then she'd pile on the pounds again when she returned to her usual routine of chocolate bars and 'beige stodge'
Her enviably slender figure has shrunk by more than four dress sizes, from a 16 to an 8 or 10. Her near-lifelong migraines have vanished, as have those limiting menopause symptoms.
And most importantly of all? She is now running around the park with her grandchildren, no longer stuck on a bench at the sidelines.
But what is extraordinary is that Becky achieved it – and she says this almost apologetically – 'without really trying'.
There was no restrictive diet, no calorie counting, and no pangs of hunger. Instead, Becky overhauled her diet with the help of gut health science company ZOE, co-founded by Professor Tim Spector, the scientist at the forefront of discoveries in diet and gut health and their impact on our overall health – and, research increasingly suggests, our mood.
Hi, I'm Professor Tim Spector, a medical scientist at King's College London, co-founder of ZOE and author of Good Mood Food.
I've spent decades researching how the food we eat affects our weight, mood and brain health. Now I'd like to share what I've discovered with you.
My exclusive six-week ZOE diet plan will show you how to eat your way to better health, with delicious recipes, simple changes and no calorie counting.
You could even lose up to a stone in time for the Christmas party season. And for DailyMail+ subscribers, it's completely free.
Click here to sign up and start your six-week ZOE diet
Research by Professor Spector, an honorary consulting physician and expert in epidemiology at King's College London, suggests that simple changes to our food choices can have remarkable benefits – from helping us lose weight without going hungry to improving our mood, boosting energy and potentially protecting our brains against the effects of ageing.
And now, in an exclusive new six-week newsletter series launching on Monday, October 26, the Daily Mail's readers can discover how to put his research into practice – with the chance to feel happier and healthier within days, and potentially as a bonus even lose up to a stone in time for Christmas.
Based on Professor Spector’s research at ZOE, and including recipes from his new cookbook Good Mood Food, the series will guide you, step-by-step, through a new way of eating that could transform not just your waistline, but most importantly how you feel every day.
You'll discover the surprisingly simple foods that nourish the trillions of bacteria living in your gut, why these microbes may hold the key to better mood and brain health, and how to feed them.
We'll show you what to put in your shopping basket – and what to leave on the shelves – and how to build delicious, filling meals.
There will be exclusive recipes, from hearty breakfasts and satisfying dinners to indulgent desserts, along with expert advice on eating to support your mood and thinking as you get older.
Halfway through, Professor Spector will make a live appearance on dailymail.com to answer readers' questions and talk about his cookbook.
And as Christmas approaches he'll reveal how to enjoy your favourite festive foods without undoing all your hard work – and, crucially, how to make these changes stick for life.
Indeed, research by Professor Spector's gut health company ZOE found that 35 per cent of around 5,000 participants lost at least 5 per cent of their body weight in just three months.
Their approach to diet has become a global phenomenon, refined through years of research involving hundreds of thousands of people.
Although more personalised recommendations are available to ZOE subscribers, anyone can follow the basic principles, for free.
Becky overhauled her diet with the help of nutrition science company ZOE, co-founded by Professor Tim Spector, the scientist at the forefront of discoveries in diet and gut health
These include eating 30 different plants a week, by making simple tweaks such as sprinkling seeds, nuts or fresh herbs over a salad or soup, or adding chopped fruit or greens to a plate.
Professor Spector encourages dieters to swap meat, particularly processed meat such as sausages, bacon and salami, for plant-based proteins including beans, lentils and chickpeas, and to aim for at least 30g of fibre a day.
However, chicken, lean meat and especially oily fish can still be enjoyed as part of his approach.
Ultra-processed foods, or UPFs – industrially-produced foods lacking in nutrients and containing cosmetic additives designed to make food irresistible to eat – are discouraged.
Instead, meals should be based on whole foods, with a rainbow of different-coloured plants to maximise nutrients.
'Studies have found that people who eat healthy diets, full of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, significantly improve their mood,' Professor Spector says.
'On the other hand, people who eat the most UPFs such as crisps, biscuits, sausages, sugary soft drinks, chicken nuggets and sugary cereal, have the biggest risk of mental health problems and dementia.
'When people have moderate depression, giving them a gut-friendly diet can improve or reverse symptoms in a significant proportion of them.'
Despite this, processed foods such as baked beans, Weetabix and high-fibre or seeded bread are on the menu.
Fermented foods, including natural yogurt, sourdough bread, kefir, sauerkraut, kombucha and kimchi, also have a role to play, as do dark chocolate and peanut butter. Most of these feature in the cookbook.
'It's not about restriction or cutting out all processed foods,' he explains, 'it's about cutting back on the worst unhealthy ultra-processed foods and replacing them with real whole plants'.
Eating more whole foods increases fibre intake – nine in ten Britons fail to get the recommended 30g a day, which can help protect against bowel cancer, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
All ZOE studies to date have shown improvements in mood and energy within the first two weeks in the majority of people.
High-fibre foods also make you feel fuller for longer and can stimulate the release of GLP-1, the appetite-regulating hormone mimicked by weight-loss drugs.
Becky, now 52, is proof of how powerful these changes can be – with benefits she never expected.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made himself President Trump’s “very good friend” and lobbied the administration to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China while he was allegedly ensnared in a Chinese honeytrap, a timeline of his reported relationship with Alice Huang shows.
The $150 billion AI boss appeared in loved-up snaps with accused communist spy Alice Huang last year — and then weeks later personally pitched Trump at the White House on relaxing export restrictions for the company’s chips.
Huang missed Trump’s second inauguration, but then more than made up for it with a $25 million donation to the president’s ballroom project.
The 63-year-old appeared at a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025, where he pushed to lift chip restrictions that had just been imposed. There were at least three documented meetings between Trump and Huang where the administration responded with policy changes that made it easier for Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
China hawks have long pushed to restrict the most cutting edge chips from the communist regime in an attempt to blunt its technological advances and stymie its attempts to overtake the US on AI.
Huang, for his part, had lobbied and spoken out against restrictions since the Biden administration first imposed limits in 2022. Additionally, selling more chips to the world’s second largest economy could only help Nvidia’s bottom line.
But all the while, Huang — who has been married to college sweetheart Lori for more than 40 years — was meeting with 42-year-old Alice. In May 2025, they were spotted at dinner together during Taiwan’s top tech expo, where she looked at him adoringly and affectionately touched his arm as they sat with other tech honchos.
Alice Huang — a TV host, turned banker, turned executive at the Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed — met Jensen Huang (no relation) in early 2024, according to reports. Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars in chips from Nvidia for data centers in Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
Separately, the firm — backed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba — is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips to China. The US government is probing reports that 50,000 chips sold to Megaspeed were seemingly missing following an audit.
Nvidia reportedly intervened in that probe, according to Bloomberg.
The Chinese government denies allegations of a honeypot spy scheme. Megaspeed also denies allegations of wrongdoing.
Trump himself has downplayed Huang’s admission of infidelity and Nvidia’s board said the company, which has no succession plan for replacing Huang, had full confidence in him, even as it announced it was investigating the claims.
On Monday, Trump said he called to check on Huang after he admitted cheating on his wife and apologized to his family.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Trump said at the White House. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him.”
The president and the Nvidia “have become good friends,” a source close to them told The Post.
Huang has made himself an integral part of the US economy. Nvidia reached a historic $5.5 trillion in valuation in May 2026, beating out Apple at the time as the most valuable public company in the entire world. It is both the world’s most important chipmaker, and the locus around which the AI boom spins. It uses the profits from its sales to help fund AI companies building out data centers, spurring further demand for its products.
By some accounts the AI boom is expected to account for up to 4% of all US economic activity this year, and Nvidia’s revenues alone up to 1%.
Trump personally hailed Nvidia’s latest quarter record sales of $96.2 billion in September, up 106% from last year.
Huang notably traveled with the president during his trip to China last May, with Trump even going as far as to personally invite the Nvidia boss to ride with him on Air Force One.
When Huang couldn’t make it to Washington DC in time for departure, he took his private plane to Alaska to join the president during his refueling stop in Anchorage.
Dressed in his signature black leather jacket and carrying only a backpack, Jensen boarded the presidential plane alone, without an entourage, pausing to speak with Trump’s son Eric, who was also on the trip, as he boarded.
Huang and his wife were seated at the head table with the president and first lady Melania Trump at the September state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping . Trump was personally involved in selecting the guest list for that dinner, a source familiar with the planning told The Post.
Along with the gains for his company, Huang’s relationship with Trump reportedly came with some perks of power.
Huang called the president when his invitation to the April state dinner for King Charles arrived without a plus one, according to a source. The billionaire CEO wanted to bring his wife to the dinner.
When White House staff told him there were no plus ones, he called Trump and made a personal appeal, getting Lori Huang on the list and bumping a senior administration official off of it to make room for her, multiple administration sources told The Post.
Huang has two grown children with his wife, Spencer and Madison, who both work in their father’s company.
The family has a $38 million home in San Francisco , with Nvidia spending nearly $4 million in fiscal 2026 on services for Huang that included home security, protection during personal travel, consulting and drivers, according to its May proxy filing.
Huang has remained close to Trump, literally, traveling to the Middle East for Trump’s visit to Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates in May 2025, then to London to join the president at Windsor Castle for a state dinner with King Charles that September.
Trump, at a meeting with then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer during that visit, saw the CEO in the audience and teasingly told him: “You’re taking over the world Jensen. I don’t know what you’re doing here. I hope you’re right.”
He also had a prime seat at Trump’s side at the September 29th meeting on AI policy , alongside other technology executives. And the president awarded him the National Medal of Science last month.
Huang and Trump remained close friends despite the warning signs about the Nvidia boss’ relationship with Alice, which one tech company flagged to the Commerce Department last summer.
“The White House has known how suspicious Ms. Huang, and her corporate network, is since last summer,” a source familiar with the case told The Post. “And Jensen has repeatedly lied about his relationship with Ms. Huang.”
Culper Research also published a report titled “NVIDIA (NVDA): The China Problem” in May 2026, which specifically warned about the concerning rumors about Nvidia’s chief executive and Alice.
Alice had been under investigation since the Biden administration and believed to have been recruited as an asset for China’s feared Ministry of State Security.
The Commerce Department first flagged Alice following her sudden rise to the top of Megaspeed in 2023.
The concerns were troubling enough that Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed back on letting Huang attend the China state dinner with Trump, the source added.
Little is known about the alleged spy’s private life, but before entering the world of finance, Alice had worked as a reporter for CCTV, the national broadcaster of the Chinese state, and Hunan TV, a regional broadcaster in central China, according to her LinkedIn biography.
Local reports claimed Alice is married to former Shanghai Hexi chairman Kang Wei — a former business partner, whose firm was fined $2.7M and censured by the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

articles.title_zh: Trade Desk’s Earnings Beat Defies Analysts’ ‘Lost Year’ Projections
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Shares of The Trade Desk (NASDAQ:TTD) charged sharply higher on Monday, surging as much as 16.6%. As of 11:38 a.m. ET, the stock was still up 15.2%.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
The catalyst that sent the digital advertising stock higher was anticipation regarding the company's upcoming financial report and the return of one of its founders.
Image source: Getty Images.
The Trade Desk announced last week that former chief technology officer (CTO) and co-founder Dave Pickles was returning after stepping down in 2023. Pickles will establish and lead the company's newly formed CTO council to "help shape the next generation of The Trade Desk platform." Pickles will focus "on aligning technology strategy, architectural direction, operational excellence, and key engineering investments--including agentic capabilities and advanced AI-powered advertising workflows."
Pickles is returning at a critical time for The Trade Desk. The company has floundered over the past year as slowing growth and increasing competition have weighed on its results. In the second quarter, The Trade Desk delivered revenue that grew just 3% year over year to $715 million, while its adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.34 slumped 17%.
Perhaps even more concerning was the company's outlook, which called for revenue to decline 12% year over year to $650 million, while adjusted EBITDA of $160 million is expected to plunge 50%.
The return of Pickles has given investors hope that The Trade Desk can return to its former glory, but they may be getting ahead of themselves.
That said, the stock is trading for just 18 times earnings, near an all-time low set just last month. Given the pessimism built into the stock price, it wouldn't take much to send The Trade Desk higher -- as evidenced by its movement today.
We'll know more soon, as The Trade Desk is scheduled to report its Q3 results after the market close today.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.
While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.
Danny Vena, CPA has positions in The Trade Desk. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends The Trade Desk. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

articles.title_orig: Brent at $90 a Barrel as Trump Plays Down Need For Further Iran Strikes
articles.title_zh: Brent at $90 a Barrel as Trump Plays Down Need For Further Iran Strikes
articles.content_orig:
Brent crude drops below $90 and markets climb after president downplays prospect of further strikes
Business live – latest updates
Oil prices have fallen to the lowest level since late August while stock markets climbed higher, as markets reacted with relief to Donald Trump saying that the war on Iran is “effectively over” .
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell nearly 3% to $89.66, the lowest since 31 August, on Tuesday morning, after the US president downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”. The fall came after a near 6% drop on Monday on signs that the conflict might be nearing an end.
Europe’s benchmark Stoxx 600 index gained 0.9% to 662.54, hovering near a record high, which it had hit in early August on hopes for a peace deal in the Middle East.
Airline stocks rose amid hopes that easing tensions could lead to lower fuel costs, with Lufthansa 1.8% ahead and Air France-KLM up 1.2%.
In London, the FTSE 100 index climbed 45 points, or 0.4%, to 10,828. The oil companies BP and Shell were the biggest losers, down 1.7% and 1.5% respectively.
During a White House press conference, Trump said Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at the trading platform Capital.com, said: “Global markets are extending their recovery this morning after Wall Street recorded a strong session that was relatively broad-based, supported by a sharp decline in oil prices and renewed buying in technology stocks.”
However, the US Federal Reserve will want more evidence of slowing inflation, she said. The latest US inflation data for October will be released at 1.30pm GMT.
Hathorn added: “Ultimately, markets are benefiting from an improvement in the geopolitical outlook, but the underlying macroeconomic and corporate risks remain unresolved. Lower energy prices could help ease inflation expectations, but the Fed will need evidence of broader disinflation before reconsidering its policy stance.
after newsletter promotion
“The key question is whether today’s inflation figures support the recovery or remind investors that resilient economic growth and persistent price pressures could keep borrowing costs elevated for longer. With technology valuations still sensitive to yields, another inflation surprise could quickly bring volatility back into focus.”
Drivers will hope the fall in wholesale oil prices continues to feed through to prices at the pump.
The AA said on Monday at the average UK petrol price has fallen 5p a litre since early October, to 169.7p a litre, and that wholesale markets indicated that another 10p reduction should be on the way.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls
articles.content_orig:
By ANDREW JEHRING, CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT and JOHN-PAUL FORD ROJAS, DEPUTY BUSINESS EDITOR
Published: 19:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 22:08 EST, 9 November 2026
The Chinese 'spy' accused of honey-trapping the boss of the world's biggest AI chip firm had bragged that she could secure his firm's technology despite a US export ban.
Alice Huang pitched a deal to Beijing investors to secure Nvidia's coveted graphics processing units (GPUs) last year.
Ms Huang said she had 'no problem securing GPUs', the Financial Times reported, even though Chinese firms are barred from obtaining them by the US.
She did not disclose her relationship with Nvidia's married chief executive Jensen Huang, who is no relation, during the investment pitch for a data centre project in Singapore .
Washington imposed strict limits on the US firm's exports to thwart attempts by Chinese president Xi Jinping to become the leading AI superpower by 2030.
Nvidia went into meltdown on Monday after Mr Huang admitted having an affair with Ms Huang months after she was declared a Chinese spy by US intelligence.
On Sunday, the 63-year-old said in a memo to staff: 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.'
The company has commissioned an independent probe into the affair. It lost around £292billion of its value – or 9 per cent – in minutes on Monday, equal to the combined value of HSBC and Barclays. Its shares recovered, but it was still down by 4 per cent by the evening, making it worth around £3trillion.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang is pictured at a party with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang in June 2024
Mr Huang admitted he was 'unfaithful' to his wife, Lori Huang, who he is pictured with her during a visit to the White House on September 24
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies.
Within a year the previously dormant firm became the largest buyer of Nvidia's chips in south-east Asia. Weeks before they started purchasing the chips she was seen drinking whisky with Taiwan-born American businessman Mr Huang in Taipei – the first known pictures of them together.
Megaspeed's imports topped £3.6billion as it opened facilities across south-east Asia and rented the firm's technology to the Chinese tech giant Alibaba.
The investments set off alarm bells in Washington and Ms Huang was placed under surveillance at the end of 2024. Earlier this year she was named as a spy in a US intelligence report.
However, Donald Trump – a close ally of Mr Huang – did nothing, the New York Times reported.
Theresa Fallon, director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies in Brussels, said: 'It is always amazing to see how so-called intelligent people fall for a Chinese honey-trap.'
Rush Doshi, an assistant security studies professor at Georgetown University in Washington, said: 'If the reporting is right, this is the most significant story in US-China policy in years.
'If the US knew Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese spy and looked the other way, all while that spy ran a company backdooring US compute to China, it warrants a Congressional investigation.'
America restricted firms from exporting advanced Nvidia chips to China in 2022, but some smuggled them illegally over the border. Others legally set up businesses that buy large numbers of chips to build data centres in south-east Asia that serve Chinese firms.
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies
Mr Huang is pictured with President Donald Trump last month
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, appeared to be a middle man, buying Nvidia chips and providing computing power to Chinese firms operating outside the country. However, it was suspected of smuggling the tech into China.
Mr Huang lobbied Mr Trump to relax export laws on chips, and when a US delegation visited China last May he was initially left off the list due to concerns about his 'influence on the President's policy of only lightly regulating AI'.
Silicon Valley giants defended the tech tycoon last night. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, a tech investment firm, tweeted that Mr Huang was 'irreplaceable for America's AI leadership', adding: 'My guess is there was no bad intention.' SpaceX boss Elon Musk said: 'I agree.'
Wall Street hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said: 'Jensen Huang is human. And he is an incredible human... even incredible humans make mistakes.'
China denied Ms Huang was a spy and accused the US of 'groundless smears and slanders'.
Nvidia said it 'prioritises US national and economic security' but 'has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
It added that Mr Huang was co-operating with its investigation and would remain as chief executive pending the review.

articles.title_orig: What we know about the mystery woman at the center of Nvidia's spy scandal
articles.title_zh: What we know about the mystery woman at the center of Nvidia's spy scandal
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares edged higher in premarket trading Tuesday as investors continued to weigh the potential fallout from CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares closed more than 4% lower on Monday, the day after Huang told staff in an email that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife and had "fallen short" of his responsibilities as CEO.
He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed , an Nvidia customer. The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that U.S. officials had concluded she was "a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing" and "possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China."
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating .
"I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago," Trump told reporters at the White House . "We'll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape."
The stock was trading 1.8% higher as of 4:40 a.m. ET.
— CNBC's Dan Mangan helped contribute to this report.
